- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.5) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% relative to prior peak or mean.
- If model shows sharp upward spike in forecast (e.g., >+5% from prior 7-day average), it often overshoots; cap forecast at 1–2% below recent high or adjust downward by 0.5–1.5 standard deviations.
- In low-sentiment periods (sentiment ≤0.2), model underestimates; increase forecast by 0.5–1.5% to align with historical mean reversion toward prior 14-day average.
- Model often lags in early periods (e.g., first 5–7 days of forecast) — adjust by adding 0.5–1.0% to early forecast values to account for delayed reaction.
- When sentiment rises sharply (e.g., from 0.0 to 0.8+ in 3–5 days), model fails to capture momentum; increase forecast by 1–2% for next 3–5 days to reflect sentiment acceleration.
- If model consistently forecasts below true outcome in 3–5 consecutive days, apply mean reversion: add 0.5–1.0% to forecast to align with 14-day moving average.
- In high-sentiment periods, avoid over-optimistic forecasts; cap forecast at 1–2% below 30-day high to prevent overcorrection.
